blocks.text: 1. Introduction

Picture two arrays sitting in front of you. One is a stack of 32 photos, each one 128 pixels tall, 128 pixels wide, with 3 color channels. The other is a spreadsheet of 500 customers with 10 columns of features each. Both are just NumPy arrays. Both are made of plain numbers. But if you tried to swap them into each other place in your code, everything would break instantly.

The reason you can tell these two arrays apart, and the reason your code can tell them apart too, comes down to three attributes that every single ndarray carries around with it: .ndim, .shape, and .size. They are not optional metadata you can ignore. They are the first thing you should look at whenever you are confused about what an array actually contains.

This lesson is short on purpose. These three attributes are simple once you see them side by side, and the goal here is to make checking them a reflex, something you do without even thinking about it, every single time you touch a new array.

items: .ndim answers "how many axes does this array have."
.shape answers "how long is each of those axes."
.size answers "how many individual numbers are in here, total."

blocks.text: 2. ndim: How Many Axes Does This Array Have

The number of dimensions, or ndim, tells you how many axes you need to walk through to reach a single number inside the array. A plain number needs zero axes, you are already looking at it. A list needs one axis, you walk along it. A grid needs two axes, you pick a row then a column. A stack of grids needs three axes, and so on.

code.content:
import numpy as np

scalar = np.array(7)
print(scalar.ndim)   # 0, nothing to walk through, it is just one number

blocks.text: Zero dimensions feels strange the first time you see it, but it makes sense once you say it out loud: a scalar has no axis at all, there is nowhere to index into, you already have the number.

code.content:
vector = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(vector.ndim)   # 1, one axis to walk along

blocks.text: One axis, one direction to move in. You can go to position 0, position 1, and so on, but that is the only kind of movement available.

code.content:
matrix = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
print(matrix.ndim)   # 2, one axis for rows, one axis for columns

blocks.text: Two axes now, rows and columns. To land on one number you need two coordinates, a row position and a column position, the same way you would point at a single cell in a spreadsheet.

code.content:
tensor = np.zeros((2, 3, 3))
print(tensor.ndim)   # 3, think of this as a small stack of matrices

blocks.text: Three axes means you now need three coordinates, which one matrix in the stack, which row, which column. This is the shape you would get from stacking two 3 by 3 matrices on top of each other.

blocks.alt: A progression from a scalar with ndim 0, to a vector with ndim 1, to a matrix with ndim 2, to a tensor with ndim 3
blocks.caption: Each step up adds one more axis you need to walk through to reach a single number.

blocks.title: ndim is about structure, not size
blocks.content: A vector with 4 numbers and a vector with 4 million numbers both have ndim 1. Dimension count tells you how the numbers are arranged, it says nothing at all about how many of them there are. Do not confuse ndim with size, they answer completely different questions.

blocks.text: 2.1 Where Higher ndim Shows Up in Real ML Code

Most everyday NumPy work lives comfortably at ndim 1 or ndim 2, single feature vectors and batches of tabular rows. But once you start working with images, video, or sequence models, higher ndim becomes completely normal, and you need to be ready for it.

Once you know this, an unfamiliar shape stops being scary, you can just count the axes and reason about what each one probably means.
3. shape: The Tuple That Describes Every Axis

If .ndim tells you how many axes an array has, .shape tells you exactly how long each one of those axes is. It is a tuple of integers, one integer per axis, always listed in the same order the axes appear in.

code.content:
scalar = np.array(7)
vector = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
matrix = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
tensor = np.zeros((2, 3, 3))

print(scalar.shape)   # ()
print(vector.shape)   # (4,)
print(matrix.shape)   # (2, 3)
print(tensor.shape)   # (2, 3, 3)

blocks.text: Count the integers inside each tuple and you will notice something: the count always matches .ndim exactly. An empty tuple means zero axes. Four numbers in the tuple means four axes. That relationship is not a coincidence, it is a rule, and section 5 makes it explicit.
3.1 Reading a Real Image Batch Shape
One of the most common shapes you will run into in computer vision work looks like this: (32, 128, 128, 3). It looks intimidating until you learn to read it left to right, one axis at a time.

items: First number, 32: the batch size, how many separate images are bundled together in this one array.
Second number, 128: the height of each image in pixels.
Third number, 128: the width of each image in pixels.
Fourth number, 3: the number of color channels, typically red, green, and blue.

blocks.alt: The shape tuple 32, 128, 128, 3 broken into four labeled boxes for batch size, height, width, and channels
blocks.caption: Batch size, height, width, channels, read left to right in that exact order.

blocks.alt: A diagram distinguishing the batch axis, which can grow or shrink, from the height, width, and channel axes, which are fixed by the image itself
blocks.caption: The batch axis is the odd one out, it changes size depending on how many images you load, the other three stay fixed.

blocks.title: Channel order is a convention, not a law
blocks.content: This lesson uses channels last, height then width then channels, which is what NumPy and TensorFlow default to. PyTorch flips this around to channels first, batch, channels, height, width. Neither one is wrong, but mixing them up is a very easy way to get a shape error, so always check which convention the library you are using expects.

blocks.text: 3.2 Reading a Tabular Features Shape
Tabular data reads the exact same way, just with fewer axes. A batch of customer records with 10 features each might come in as shape (500, 10).

First number is again how many things you have, 500 customers this time instead of 32 images. Second number is how many values describe each one, 10 features instead of height, width, and channels. The idea behind every axis is the same: how many things, and how is each thing described. Only the number of axes and what they represent changes from problem to problem.

blocks.alt: A tabular batch with shape 500 by 10 shown next to an image batch with shape 32, 128, 128, 3, both representing the same underlying idea
blocks.caption: Two very different shapes, but both answer the same two questions: how many things, and how is each one described.

blocks.text: 4. size: The Total Count of Numbers Inside
The .size attribute is the simplest of the three. It is just the total number of individual numbers stored in the array, no matter how those numbers are arranged across axes.

code.content:
scalar = np.array(7)
vector = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
matrix = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])

print(scalar.size)   # 1
print(vector.size)   # 4
print(matrix.size)   # 6, 2 rows times 3 columns

blocks.text: You may have noticed that 6 is exactly 2 times 3, the two numbers inside the matrix shape tuple. That is not a coincidence either. Size is always the product of every entry in the shape tuple, multiplied together.

blocks.alt: The four shape entries 32, 128, 128, and 3 all feeding into a multiply operation that outputs a size of 1,572,864
blocks.caption: Multiply every entry in the shape tuple together and you get the size, no exceptions.

blocks.title: Size grows fast, and memory follows it
blocks.content: That image batch shape, 32 by 128 by 128 by 3, has a size of 1,572,864 individual numbers. At 4 bytes per number for a typical float32 array, that is roughly 6 megabytes for just one batch. Double the batch size or the image resolution and the memory cost climbs just as fast. Checking .size is a quick way to catch a batch that is about to blow past your available memory before it actually happens.

blocks.text: 5. How ndim, shape, and size Fit Together
You have now seen all three attributes on their own. Here is the part that ties them together, stated as plainly as possible, because these three rules never break.

items: ndim always equals the number of entries in shape, in other words len(shape).
size always equals every entry in shape multiplied together.
Given any two of the three, you can work out useful facts about the third, they are never independent of each other.

blocks.alt: The shape tuple 32, 128, 128, 3 being counted to produce an ndim of 4
blocks.caption: ndim is not a separate fact you memorize, it falls straight out of counting the shape tuple.

code.content:
import math

arr = np.zeros((32, 128, 128, 3))

assert arr.ndim == len(arr.shape)
assert arr.size == math.prod(arr.shape)

print(arr.ndim, arr.shape, arr.size)
# 4 (32, 128, 128, 3) 1572864

blocks.alt: A diagram showing shape as the source, with an arrow to ndim labeled length of shape, and an arrow to size labeled product of shape
blocks.caption: shape is the one true source of truth, ndim and size are both just calculations derived from it.

blocks.text: 6. Shape Mismatches: The Most Common Bug in ML Code

Here is the honest truth about writing ML code day to day: the bug you will hit the most is not a subtle math mistake or a broken algorithm. It is a plain shape mismatch, two arrays that disagree about how many rows or columns they have, and an operation that has no way to make sense of the disagreement.

Matrix multiplication is the classic example. To multiply array A by array B, the number of columns in A has to match the number of rows in B. If they do not match, NumPy will not guess what you meant, it will simply refuse and raise an error.

code.content:
A = np.zeros((3, 4))
B = np.zeros((5, 2))

result = A @ B
# ValueError: matmul: Input operand 1 has a mismatch in its core dimension 0,
# with gufunc signature (n?,k),(k,m?)->(n?,m?) (size 5 is different from 4)

blocks.alt: Array A with shape 3 by 4 and array B with shape 5 by 2 both feeding into a matmul attempt that fails with a ValueError about mismatched shapes
blocks.caption: The inner numbers, 4 and 5, do not match, so the multiply cannot happen.

blocks.title: Read the error message, it already tells you the answer
blocks.content: That error message is not decoration. It spells out the exact two numbers that disagree, size 5 is different from 4 in the example above. Whenever you hit a shape error, the fastest fix is almost always to read the message slowly instead of guessing, it is usually pointing directly at the problem.

blocks.text: 6.1 What a Shape Match Actually Looks Like
Fixing the example above just means making the inner dimensions agree. A has shape (3, 4), so B needs 4 rows, not 5, for the multiply to work.

code.content:
A = np.zeros((3, 4))
B = np.zeros((4, 2))   # 4 rows now matches A columns of 4

result = A @ B
print(result.shape)   # (3, 2)

blocks.alt: Array A with shape 3 by 4 and array B with shape 4 by 2 both feeding into a working matmul that produces a result of shape 3 by 2
blocks.caption: Once the inner numbers match, 4 and 4, the outer numbers, 3 and 2, decide the shape of the result.

blocks.text: Notice the outer numbers survive into the result shape, 3 rows from A and 2 columns from B, while the matching inner numbers, both 4, disappear entirely. This inner-must-match, outer-survives pattern is worth memorizing, it explains almost every shape you will ever see come out of a matrix multiply.
6.2 Defensive Shape Checking as a Debugging Habit

The single best habit you can build while debugging ML code is boring and cheap: print .shape after every step that transforms an array. It costs almost nothing to run and it turns a confusing failure three steps later into an obvious one right where it happens.

code.content:
def preprocess(images, weights):
    print("raw images:", images.shape)
    x = images.reshape(images.shape[0], -1)
    print("flattened:", x.shape)
    out = x @ weights
    print("after weights:", out.shape)
    return out

blocks.alt: A loop diagram showing write code, run and hit an error, print dot shape, fix the mismatch, and back to write code
blocks.caption: Checking shape defensively turns an unpredictable crash into a fast, repeatable debugging loop.

items: Print .shape right before any reshape, matrix multiply, or concatenation, those are the three operations most sensitive to shape.
Leave the expected shape as a short comment next to the print statement, so a mismatch jumps out immediately.
When something breaks three functions deep, do not guess, go back and print the shape at every step until you find exactly where it went wrong.

blocks.text: 7. Reshaping Without Changing the Data

Once you know a shape is wrong for what you need, the fix is usually .reshape(). It rearranges the exact same numbers into a new shape without touching the underlying data or copying it in memory, as long as the total size stays the same.

code.content:
flat = np.arange(12)
print(flat.shape)   # (12,)

grid = flat.reshape(3, 4)
print(grid.shape)   # (3, 4)

other_grid = flat.reshape(2, 6)
print(other_grid.shape)   # (2, 6)

blocks.alt: The same 12 numbers in memory being reshaped into a 3 by 4 grid, a 2 by 6 grid, and a flat shape of 12
blocks.caption: Same 12 numbers every time, just organized differently. reshape never invents or deletes a single value.

blocks.title: reshape only works if the size matches
blocks.content: You can reshape 12 numbers into (3, 4) or (2, 6) or (12,) or (4, 3), anything whose product equals 12. Try to reshape into (5, 3), which needs 15 numbers, and NumPy will refuse immediately. Reshaping is covered in full depth in its own dedicated lesson later in this module, this is just enough to recognize it when you see it.

blocks.text: 8. Worked Example: Inspecting a Real Batch
Let us put all three attributes to work at once, side by side, on the two arrays from the very start of this lesson: a batch of images and a batch of tabular customer data.

code.content:
image_batch = np.zeros((32, 128, 128, 3))
tabular_batch = np.zeros((500, 10))

for name, arr in [("image_batch", image_batch), ("tabular_batch", tabular_batch)]:
    print(name)
    print("  ndim :", arr.ndim)
    print("  shape:", arr.shape)
    print("  size :", arr.size)

# image_batch
#   ndim : 4
#   shape: (32, 128, 128, 3)
#   size : 1572864
# tabular_batch
#   ndim : 2
#   shape: (500, 10)
#   size : 5000

blocks.text: Same three questions, two very different answers. The image batch needs four axes because it is tracking batch, height, width, and channels all at once, while the tabular batch only needs two, rows and features. Neither shape is more correct than the other, they are just describing different kinds of data, and now you have a fast, repeatable way to read either one on sight.
9. Recap

items: .ndim is the number of axes an array has, 0 for a scalar, 1 for a vector, 2 for a matrix, 3 or more for a tensor.
.shape is a tuple giving the length of every axis, in order, and its length always equals .ndim.
.size is the total count of numbers in the array, always equal to every entry in .shape multiplied together.
Shape mismatches are the most common runtime error in ML code, and reading the error message plus printing .shape is the fastest way through them.
.reshape() rearranges data into a new shape without changing the data itself, as long as the total size stays the same.

blocks.text: These three attributes will follow you into every single NumPy array you ever touch. Get in the habit of glancing at .shape the moment you load or create anything new, before you even start writing the logic that uses it. It takes one line, and it will save you far more debugging time than it costs.
